narration: S02.1 On the schedule alone, you can't even ask to cancel it for about 8 years.
S02.2 We replayed real US prices and rates month by month, so you'll see how long it took on paper, typically and in slow cases.
B02-S02.muted_read: The loan, as a share of the price, starts at 90 % and drifts down slowly; it only touches the 80 % line after about 8 years.

narration: S03.1 On paper means the loan is 80 percent of the home's value by a national price index.
S03.2 That's not the same as getting the insurance removed.
S03.3 Removal on today's value, when you ask, is the loan owner's rule; for Fannie Mae loans, that's a waiting period and a 75 percent bar.
S03.4 You'll also meet three illustrative buyers who got very different answers.
S03.5 It's US only, history, not a forecast, and it won't say whether to buy or wait.
B03-S03.muted_read: Hitting the 80 % line on paper is one line; a second, lower line (75 %, early years) and three steps (request, appraisal, wait) still stand before 'insurance removed'.
B03-S03.note: S03.3 B+2 label on screen: "Fannie Mae: wait ≥ 2 years · loan ≤ 75%" (claims value_removal_seasoning_years, value_removal_ltv_early)

narration: S06.1 At September's average mortgage rate, 6.86 percent, the monthly payment for principal and interest is the figure on screen.
S06.2 Taxes, home insurance and the mortgage insurance all come on top of it.
S06.3 Each payment pays the balance down a little, slowly at first, and faster later on.
N1-S06.muted_read: Each page of the calendar is one monthly payment ($2,362/month, principal + interest, illustrative); as the pages flip, the loan stack slides along the payments and its top draws the balance: it falls slowly at first and faster later.

narration: S07.1 By federal law, the borrower can ask to cancel the insurance once the schedule says the loan is down to 80 percent of the original value, here $320,000.
S07.2 On this loan, that's payment 99, the date this video opened with.
S07.3 That request comes with conditions, such as being current on payments.
B07-S07.muted_read: On the same falling line, a first marker sits where the loan reaches 80 % of the original price, at payment 99: 'you may ask'.

narration: S08.1 And the insurance has to end automatically when the schedule reaches 78 percent, as long as payments are current.
S08.2 Here, that's about 9.5 years in.
S08.3 Both dates come from the schedule alone, and both ignore what the house is worth.
B08-S08.muted_read: A second marker a little later, at 78 %: 'ends automatically'. Both markers sit on the payment line; the house's value is nowhere on the chart.

narration: S11.1 The typical answer: 23 months.
S11.2 Half of the purchase months got there sooner, and half took longer.
S11.3 And in 90.6 percent of them, prices got the loan to 80 percent on paper no later than the schedule would have.
S11.4 That's the gap between the schedule's long road and the replay's typical one.
B11-S11.muted_read: Most purchase months have short bars; a horizontal median line sits low at 23 months, far below a faint ridge of the schedule's own months; nearly every bar ends below its schedule mark.

narration: S12.1 But that's on paper.
S12.2 We also checked a larger set: every purchase month since January 1991 with two years of prices after it.

S12.3 Two years after purchase, only 15.6 percent of them were at or below the 75 percent bar Fannie Mae sets for its loans when a borrower asks to cancel on today's value, a separate route from the law's schedule.
S12.4 So reaching 80 percent on paper in about two years was common in this history, while clearing that early bar by then was not.
B12-S12.muted_read: Two years in, a little more than half the months are under the 80 % line, but only a thin slice is under the 75 % line lenders often use early.

narration: S13.1 The typical case also hides a long tail.
S13.2 About 1 in 7 purchase months took more than 5 years.
S13.3 They sit together in one stretch of the grid, the months just before and during the national price slump.
B13-S13-N2.muted_read: Back on the grid, the bars over 60 months turn `warn`; they are few, and they sit together in one stretch of purchase months.

narration: S14.1 The slowest was October 2005: 112 months on paper.
S14.2 That's longer than the schedule itself took at that month's rate.
S14.3 And this is a national average: no single home tracks it, and a local market can do much better or much worse.
S14.4 So why did the same rule give such different answers?
B14-S14.muted_read: The zoom frame lands on the tallest bar: bought October 2005, 112 months on paper, taller than that month's schedule mark.

narration: S16.1 Owen bought in January 2004, while prices were climbing fast.
S16.2 He reached 80 percent on paper in 13 months, the fastest in the replay.
S16.3 Rising prices did most of that work, not his payments.
B16-S16.muted_read: Owen's panel: the index line climbs steeply, and his on-paper line drops through 80 % almost at once, while his schedule line has barely moved.

narration: S17.1 [serious] Victor bought the year after Owen, in October 2005: the slowest month in the replay.
S17.2 Prices rose a little, then fell for years, and even when he finally reached 80 percent on paper, the index was still below where it started.
S17.3 He got there by paying the loan down, and his own schedule, at his lower rate of 6.07 percent, reached 80 percent of the original price first, at payment 90.
S17.4 Whether a lender would have dropped his insurance at that point, this data can't show.
B17-S17.muted_read: Victor's panel: the index line rises a little, then falls for years; his on-paper line stays above 80 % long after his schedule line has crossed it at payment 90.

narration: S18.1 Same rule, same national index: what differed was the month they started, and what prices did next.
S18.2 So a plan can be measured against two benchmarks from this history.
S18.3 One is the schedule the law uses, which on the example loan runs most of a decade.
S18.4 The other is history on paper: a plan that counts on about two years matched the typical month, not the slow ones, and not the lender's step.
S18.5 On the illustrative $400,000 home, the other path, 20 percent down, means $40,000 more up front.
S18.6 This video doesn't weigh that against renting or waiting; it measures how long the insurance math took.
